newsitem.title: CANADA: Senate may stall Canadian tobacco bill - minister.
newsitem.headline: Senate may stall Canadian tobacco bill - minister.

text.p: Canadian Health Minister David Dingwall said on Friday he had been warned that the powerful tobacco industry might try to stall his anti-tobacco legislation in the unelected Senate.
"We have been alerted, if you will, that there may be some things that will try to take place in the upper house (of Parliament)," he told reporters.

Dingwall, who told the lower House of Commons on Friday he plans to introduce the bill in the House on Monday, said he had heard that the tobacco industry was lobbying senators, hoping to turn them against the government's bill.
The Senate must ratify any legislation passed by the lower house before it becomes law. Usually it does not block government bills but it does sometimes delay them.
The package seeks to ban tobacco advertisements on radio, television or billboards; prohibit vending machine sales; and restrict the use of brand names in sponsoring sporting and other events.
The tobacco industry has charged that these measures are extreme and, possibly, illegal.
The Reform Party, one of two major opposition parties in the lower house, has indicated it would facilitate passage of the bill in order to make it law as soon as possible.
"I welcome the support of the Reform Party, I think they are being very responsible in putting partisanship aside," said Dingwall.
The three major players in the Canadian tobacco market are:
- Imperial Tobacco Ltd, a unit of Imasco Ltd, which controls about 65 percent of the Canadian cigarette market. Imasco is 40 percent owned by B.A.T. Industries Plc of Britain.
- Rothmans, Benson and Hedges Inc, owned 60 percent by Rothmans International, a unit of Rothmans International Plc, and 40 percent by Philip Morris Cos Inc.
- RJR MacDonald, wholly owned by RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp unit R.J. Reynolds Tobacco International.
